I've been playing Dota 2 for 12 years now, off and on throughout my life it is one of the few constants. In high school, my friends and I spent many nights playing when there was only one courier. In college I played once or twice a year on my rented laptop from school. During the pandemic It was a way for my brothers and I to connect when we couldn't actually visit each other. It holds a great place in my life.  [h3]The Good[/h3] - Gameplay is dynamic, engaging and rewarding once you get the hang of it. There are so many moving parts that when you make your first big play, there is very little that can match the feeling of satisfaction when played just right.  - Flourishing Pro Scene: If you want to get better there are countless new and old pro players that stream or release content on Youtube to help you improve, and often times Discord chats to find players to play with. - Semi Consistent Updates: They just released one of the biggest updates the game has seen since Talents were released in 2016, or neutral items were released in 2019, or when they DOUBLED the size of the map in 2022. Valve isn't afraid to experiment with this game, and while you can get stuck on a single patch for a long time, you can always know that Valve Devs are working on something truly different to add.  [h3]Negatives[/h3] - Mental Health: This is a team game. I love it for that, but playing with others can be frustrating and demoralizing. You can also find yourself "chain queuing" which after multiple losses can really effect your mood outside the game. My girlfriend and I have a rule that I cant start a game after 10pm because if i lose badly sometimes I will be too angry to fall asleep or talk before bed. You have to find these ways to look inward yourself, and without barriers it can really negatively impact you. - The Community: I said it a bit above, but if you're new to online games there is so much racism, sexism, anger etc. I've met really great people playing dota, but the brain tends to remember the bad eggs. Remember there is a mute button. - Communication from Valve: There can be crickets from valve sometimes. They ARE working on stuff, but if you read reddit to much you can get a bit riled for no reason.  Overall, best game I've ever played by a long margin.

Recommended 👍 | Classic, chaotic, endlessly fun  Team Fortress 2 is a masterclass in multiplayer shooters. Over a decade later, it still delivers fast-paced, team-based chaos with a perfect balance of humor and strategy.  The class system is brilliant. Each of the nine classes has a unique role, and mastering them adds endless depth. Want to sneak behind enemy lines as a Spy? Protect objectives as a Heavy? Or just rocket-jump around causing mayhem as a Soldier? The choice is yours—and every match feels different depending on who’s playing what.  Maps are iconic, gameplay is tight, and the community keeps things lively with mods, cosmetics, and custom servers. The art style and humor are timeless, making the game approachable while still rewarding skill.  Teamwork is essential. Success comes from coordination, awareness, and knowing when to push or retreat. And if the coordination falls apart… chaos ensues, often hilariously.  Pros:  Deep, varied, and fun class system  Fast-paced, strategic gameplay  Iconic maps and modes  Endlessly replayable with community support  Cons:  Community can be toxic at times  Some newer players may struggle with the skill curve  Older graphics, though charming  Final verdict: Team Fortress 2 is a timeless multiplayer experience. It’s chaotic, hilarious, and deeply rewarding when teamwork clicks. Whether you’re a veteran or a newcomer, it’s easy to jump in, have fun, and get lost in hours of mayhem.

Well after 500 hours, I think I can write up a review on this gem. I was first introduced to TF2 from the plethora of content on it. Whether that be the dumb 2008 SFM's or well thought out video essays on the intricacies on certain weapons, the content hooked me and honestly, feels like the heart of this game. After around a week of seeing people sing the praises about this game, I decided enough was enough and eventually just installed it. I instantly fell in love.  Well besides having to watch a video to fix the god awful default settings (no seriously they really suck), I was having the time of my life. I find it surprising I chose to main scout in the biggening , the "run and gun" but thinking about it some more I can understand why since he was the easiest class to learn, at least for me. Running around, shooting people and moving around at lightspeed was so addictive, however I wanted to see what the rest of the game offered. I loved the movement and damage output of the soldier, the chaotic mess of keeping your buildings up as engineer and keeping you team mates alive as medic. The simple yet also complex skill ceiling of pyro and heavy. The satisfaction of sniper and spy. It all seemed to click with me so early on in my TF2 journey that I can confidently say I've never had more fun with a game so quickly. But ultimately, I decided to main demoman due to the high skill ceiling, the raw damage, and the movement. Even though demo is my favorite, I would be lying if I said all the other classes weren't a lot of fun too. Their are so many playstyles that you are bound to find the one that suits you and I feel like that is what keeps me playing. The thought of improvement and experimentation between hundreds of loadouts is why I find this game so fun. The variety of matchups with other classes, the amazing maps (although their are waay too many maps in the game so I happen to only select less than half of them due to the map quality being very bloated).  500 hours and 9 months later, I think its safe to say that TF2 is my favorite game of all time and I now understand why so many keep retuning to this old yet somehow fresh masterpiece.

This has shot straight to my top games ever, I really really enjoy the themes of RDR and its commentary on turn-of-the-century 1900s America. Despite all their accaim, I've not actually played that many Rockstar games, with most of my exposure being through gta5.  Because of this, I thought the story would be a little bit more satirical, so it's tone surprised me in a very good way. I really like the themes of industrialisation and its impacts on both the environment and tradition (I don't think I've ever played a game that explored this so explicitly before). Its other themes regarding the morality of the law and the discussion of the consequences of immoral actions are also really well developed. This last theme really resonates with The Last of Us as well, in that I think John Marston and Joel are very similar characters as they commit, in many ways, irredemable acts, but within the confines of their own moral compass. It also reminds me a bit of Omar from the wire. I really like these sorts of characters and the exploration of grey morality and Red Dead is one of the best video game explorations of the concept I've played.  In terms of being a PC port, it's a little bit buggy, there's some stuff that definitely shows the age of the game, and I'm surprised it's as bad as it is considering it's not that much older than GTA 5 which is a really, really good PC port. I'm kind of willing to overlook this though because the actual story and the gameplay is so strong that the occasional bug is not that much of an issue (although one did cause me to have to replay the entirety of a 30 min mission which was annoying as hell). Also having the last mission be a strangers is definitely a weird choice that may mean some people miss the resolution of the game.  Anyway, now i'm really excited to play red dead redemption two. Based off this it should be another 10/10.

Read Dead Redemption is a game of its time, however, the story is wonderful. Read Dead Redemption 2 flows into Read Dead Redemption 1 so well. John Marston, similar to Arthur Morgan, is a well written and complex protagonist. There are moments where I feel Marston is even more complex. This is a story about a man's past continuously catching back up to him. When he is focused on starting a new and just when he becomes comfortable, it all comes back.   As a said earlier, the game is a product of the time when it came out. It is rough around the edges and can feel wonky at times. It would be very interesting to see a full remake of this game built within the engine of RDR2. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this. It is a very good follow through from the story of RDR2 and provides a few knots to some loose ends that were within its predecessor (by story, not release). Loved my time with it.

Replaying this again in 2026, with high resolution, high framerate, easy screenshotting and video recording on PC, is like bringing a small piece of my childhood back. It's also surprising that, after playing Red Dead 2, the story holds up this well and it's almost like they wrote it with a prequel in mind. One of the best Rockstar Games ever made, and it's basically a must-play if you enjoyed RDR2.  You play as John Marston, an ex-member of the Van Der Linde gang. Dutch's gang was something skin to the Robinhood-type of outlaws, criminals with the heart of gold. Until things went wrong and everything fell apart. If you've played RDR2, you already knew the wild and heartbreaking events of the gang had faced. John has been coerced by private investigators, most likely the Pinkerton's, to hunt down the last remaining ex-members that turned to even more violence and banditry. The story progresses quite slow at first, and each mission feels like a never-ending build-up. But as per Rockstar's tradition, it ramps up past the midway point and everything becomes super intense and action-packed. The atmosphere and music help sell the lonely wild west setting and narrative greatly as well. Overall it's a very well written story with memorable moments and characters. But if you've played the prequel, it becomes even better and hits you even harder.  Another reason I enjoyed this a lot is the gameplay. Despite being almost 16 years old now, it still holds up super well. It strikes the perfect balance between snappy gameplay of the older games and the quality of life that newer entries bring. The openworld feels a bit small, now that we have plenty of other great open world games to compare. But the well-placed side missions and differences of each region completely make the modest map size a non-issue. With all that mentioned, it has some sequence-breaking bugs that will have you reloading saves maybe 4-5 times throughout the playthrough. It's not that bad but certainly an annoyance, especially during high-stake story missions.  Definitely a recommend, especially if you've played Red Dead 2 and interested in learning what happens next. It might not look as pretty as the prequel, but following the story of John after breaking off from the Van Der Linde's in this moderately-sized adventure and smooth gameplay experience is absolutely worth it.

Grand Theft Auto V Enhanced builds on the foundation of the Legacy edition and elevates it in nearly every meaningful way, creating the definitive single-player and offline experience of GTA V. The Enhanced version brings technical upgrades that harness modern hardware — higher resolutions, improved textures, better draw distances, more detailed character models, more dynamic lighting, and smoother performance even in dense urban environments. These upgrades make returning to Los Santos feel like playing a whole new game, especially if your last playthrough was on older hardware.  But the enhancements go beyond visuals. Enhanced improves how the world feels: denser traffic and pedestrian populations, richer environmental detail, and subtle yet impactful improvements to weather, reflections, and animation polish. The game benefits from advancements in physics, draw distances, and performance that make both high-speed chases and quiet exploration feel more immersive. These upgrades matter — the same content that was great before feels crisper and more alive now.  Content remains vast: the same sprawling campaign, heists, side missions, collectibles, races, properties, and myriad activities that defined the Legacy version are all present — but now with a sheen that elevates the experience. Owning multiple properties, running businesses, and collecting everything from stunt jumps to hidden packages still gives you hundreds of hours of structured progression. Even without stepping into GTA Online, there’s a staggering amount of content here for solo players craving both structured goals and emergent chaos.  If you loved the original GTA V experience, the Enhanced edition refines it in every direction — visually, technically, and atmospherically — without sacrificing the enormous sandbox content that keeps players invested for hundreds of hours. It’s a testament to how much life Rockstar built into this world that it can feel fresh even years later.  — The Ember Archives https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45601239/

Years ago I tried playing through the story on what is now the "legacy" version. This time I did sit through the whole thing, but I was very often being reminded of why I never finished it in the first place. I didn't play through all the side content. I did a few side missions. They were pretty funny, but they get old quickly, so I couldn't be bothered. I wanted to see the main story, the characters development. It is a pretty okay story I guess. Very hollywood action/crime movie style with corrupt government agents, mercenaries and all kinds of crooks. A lot of things are obviously designed in a way to be as offensive as possible and tiptoeing around crossing the line or not. That's nothing new in GTA. For the most part it's all in good fun with the names of stores and corporations in the world. Some things can make you chuckle a little bit, but for the most part I don't really care. I only visited stores when I had to, so when a mission objective said to go to a store and buy something. Other than that it's completely unnecessary. I never ran out of ammo, so why go to Ammunation all the time? Each protagonist has their own character correct clothing, so why visit clothing stores all the time? The personal vehicles of each protagonist are always fixed and at their safe houses when you left them somewhere, so there is also very little reason to visit Los Santos Customs... Anybody reading this will get the point by now. I also don't really care about the whole GTA Online stuff... There's too many cheaters and griefers on there to have any fun anyway, so why bother?  So... The main story. It's fine I guess. It offers quite a lot of variation in missions and the big heists with the whole setup thing going on is pretty good. Lester is a fun character and the way the planning is presented is fun. You get to choose the approach, then choose a bunch of henchmen and have at it. Each of the 3 protagonists also have their own side stories that also have to be completed for the main story to progress. This gives some extra depth to the characters, which is nice. The characters themselves though... The 3 protagonists... Franklin the stereotypical gangbanger, Michael the classic movie style gangster and Trevor the drug and weapons dealing psychopath. They all have their good things, but for the most part they are the least likeable protagonist characters I have ever seen in a videogame. When Franklin is talking with his buddy Lamar, every third word in the conversation is the N-word which I'm obviously not going to spell out here. I see what they tried to do here, but it gets old really fast. Michael is just a self righteous prick and he only gets worse in that regard as the story progresses. Trevor is funny at first, but his constant yelling and his extremely abusive demeanor get old fairly quickly. He also doesn't have much of a redemption arc or anything of the sort and after a while I found him to be more obnoxious than funny. Most of the antagonist characters are very typical movie villains. Devin Weston the rich prick who screws everybody over and Steve Haines the corrupt federal agent. These are the main antagonists. They are predictable and mostly uninteresting. Was it worthit to actually play through the whole main story? Not really. Very unlikely I'll ever do it again.  Aside from the story, the gameplay is obviously the most important aspect of a game. For the most part it's fine. It's nothing earth shattering. Elements of it go on a scale from okay to serviceable. Car handling is pretty good. Motorcyle handling as well. Boat handling is fine too and so it airplane handling. Helicopter handling though... That is a nightmare. I guess they had to make a choice between making that either very simple or very complicated. They chose something inbetween and it's not good. The helicopter always drifting in a certain direction combined with the camera snapping back to it's rear when you're constantly moving to a top down view to try and line it up is a major head ache. Because of this I avoided using helicopters as much as I could. It doesn't have to be as simplistic as it is in Saints Row 3 for example, but the way it is in this game prevents helicopter flying from being fun. The controls on the map screen are very counter intuitive and it always feels like it's moving in the opposite direction of what you want. At least when you're using a mouse. It feels very much like it was designed with gamepad controls in mind and they didn't bother to test how it works on PC with a mouse. The combat feels very mediocre, but it gets the job done for the most part. Never does the combat actually feel challenging. Stealth is a fun concept, but very poorly executed and it's only relevant a handful of times anyway. The map is huge and most of it is completely empty. Size over substance. The city itself is pretty cool to look at, but the rest of the map is mostly empty space. The size of the map was a major marketing point when this game was new. What they accomplished with such a large map is mostly a lot of long driving sections where you do nothing besides driving and the banter between characters is over when you're halfway there (with a few exceptions where the banter was so long that they were still yapping when already standing still for 5 minutes just in front of the destination). It all looks pretty good, especially for a game that is already 13 years old. The enhanced edition made some very noticable improvements to the visuals as well. The first person mode is also a pretty cool feature, but it feels so incredibly floaty that I quickly switched back to the default third person camera. It's cool that it's there, but I feel like they should commit to it and make it actually good or just stick with third person.  I realise that the tone of most of this piece of text is pretty negative, but it's not a bad game overall. It's just not all that great either. I was reminded a lot of why I never finished it years ago and decided I had to give it another shot and actually finish it. So that's what I did. I also don't have high hopes for GTA6. It's map will likely be even bigger with even more empty space to do nothing and even longer pointless and long car rides to pad out the length.

Really great opportunity for role playing expression with character creation and build variety. 5. Barely any cutscenes, and the ones that are there are like ~30 seconds. 6. Really well-optimized at this point and can run on a lot of hardware (3 kids and no money kinda rigs or no kids and 3 money kinda rigs). 7. Great challenge that isn't too cheesy so you don't feel like you're wasting your limited gaming time, but also feels rewarding (yes, even PCR). 8. Stakes of Marika eliminate stupidly painful runbacks.  Elden Ring is now my favorite game of all time. It's a From Software game which as a result inherits many of the good mechanics from the Dark Souls series and forms a great base for gameplay however it is ruined by the addition of the needless open world design. The world feels empty and did not make new game plus enjoyable through its repetitive dungeons and reuse of bosses as common enemies. The disuse of previous linear and interconnected design of Dark Souls negatively impacted the game's travelling and discourages normal traversal of the world in favour of the fast travel system.   The PvP scene is very lively albeit highly over tuned, power-stancing certain weapons such as great spears deals far too much damage, in addition, many spells and weapons seem far too powerful comparatively to the rest of the roster leading to fights being repetitive. Whilst some weapon such as rivers of blood received a rightful nerf, it seems to have inherent balance issues.   The boss fights in this game whilst visually stunning, relies heavily on delayed attacks intertwined with normal attacks or attacks requiring the player to stay in a safe zone or risk an instant death, an example being Malenia. Not every boss displays these attack types however it seems that, from the base roster, and the new DLC, that From Software has favoured such boss designs over the conventional ones found in previous games such as Bloodborne or Dark Souls. The community's common response of "Git Gud" focuses on the difficulty rather than inherent boss design, ignoring that memorising attack patterns can be done by anyone and a person who did successfully beat a boss may have criticisms of its design nonetheless.   TLDR: Game STINKS

Horizon 5 is such a strange game to talk about, because while I'd say it's the best game in the series it has loads of flaws many of which have been carried forward from previous entries, sometimes over a decade old.  Mexico (and Sierra Nueva in the dlc) is an absolutely beautiful map, from the desert to the jungles to the volcano, to the mountain and the valley, to Guanajuato the extremely vibrant city. But a large portion of the map is just fields, and these fields make up the central area of the map where players are most likely to pass through. All of the amazing features of Mexico are concentrated around the outer edges of the map, and Guanajuato itself is also terribly small.   The story is bad. Awful, even. Previous entries didn't have a good story either but (aside from 4 which this is a direct sequel to) they were bad in the normal racing game way, that is to say you could just ignore it and nobody cares because we're here to race cars. Here it's just, so so so so terribly grating. Endless empty corporate positivity everywhere, the speaking of what I think was an attempt at spanglish? in a way that absolutely nobody has ever spoken. It didn't even seem out of place when I got to the hot wheels dlc and Haley just spoke advertisements for toys at me the entire time because really that's just the next logical step when your characters sit somewhere between middle management, HR personnel, and that one pepsi commercial with the riot police.  Cars are good, there's a lot of them. For the first time in the series the mods you put on can effect your engine's sound so you can audibly hear the difference between things like the exhaust options. The new handling model is rather great, though it does feel like it leads to annoying levels of oversteer on RWD cars at times. An annoying amount of cars are stuck behind wheelspins or whatever live service thing they wanted to shove in for no reason, though. Seriously you could just buy the Trueno immediately in 1-3 why have 4 and 5 decided to banish it to live service purgatory.  Unlike in 4 you can't set back the date on your computer to get old series rewards, if you're not connected to the internet it just pays out wheelspins as rewards instead. This is stupid and bad, why are you locking cars behind the auction house? There's not even a profit motive for it which makes it even stranger.  The PI system is still bad and extremely easy to game, because of the way it's calculated you can do things like have an AWD swap that costs almost nothing or cram an absurd amount of power into a given class cap because the AI driver used to calculate scores by driving it around a simulated test track always uses the default tune, so you can do things like adjust sway bars to fix understeer or adjust the gearing ratio to actually be able to use all of that power and it won't have any sort of impact on your car's class despite it clearly being much better than what the simulation suggests. This also makes online racing much less satisfying, because even without relying on these quirks to make a better build than what should be possible you can still end up with major performance discrepancies between the two PI numbers, and it can start to feel less like you're winning/losing due to skill differences and more like it's just a simple gap between the cars. Winning because I can corner better and at higher speeds is fun, winning because my car can corner better and go faster isn't.  Progression is basically nonexistent, you do races and then pick whatever story thing you wanna do next whether it's a showcase race where the rigging to be a photo finish has never been more obvious or an expedition where you drive around a closed off area of the map smashing stuff (these are still fun though). It's all entirely disconnected from me actually playing the game. There's no car class or type limitations on anything. If you wanna go through the entire game in nothing but the 2020 supra they give you at the start you can. Actually there is one limitation and that's with the midnight battles, which were added in a post-launch update and there's only 4.  Speaking of disconnected from me actually playing the game, wheelspins. Introduced in 2 (4 added junk item like horns and clothes to the pool) they're just lootboxes (you can't pay money for them though). You get either a random car, a random amount of money from 5-300k, a random piece of clothing, or a new car horn sound. Get unlucky on a wheelspin, you get basically nothing. Get lucky and suddenly you've gained either a car that sells for a substantial amount on the auction house or a bunch of credits, about 20 race's worth. At any given time I tend to be sitting on 1-3m in credits and an insignificant amount of these are actually earned via skilled racing. There's no accomplishment felt when buying one of the more expensive cars because I didn't actually *do* anything to earn it, I just got lucky on a lottery.  The livery editor and the vinyl maker are largely the same as they've been since 2. Gran Turismo has had SVG importing options since Sport which released in 2017, before Horizon 4 came out.  The AI cheats massively, if first and second can get away by the fourth corner you just restart the race because they're going to continue getting faster and faster to the point you can't catch up. Conversely if you get out in front the race is a time attack as the AI will make no attempts to overtake and will instead slowly fall further and further behind until half the pack DNFs. They have much better grip than the player and also follow the racing line extremely closely even when it's wrong, so the player can easily overtake in corners where they brake entirely too much (most noticeable on dirt or the hot wheels races)   Road, Street, and Dirt races all have mostly good layouts, and 5's new physics model makes dirt super fun to race on as well, so my only major critique here is dear god why are there so many walls. It's hard to take the McRae approach to rally when sliding slightly off the road actually means slamming in to the solid concrete wall set up right at the edge of every single corner. Also gives rise to wall riding, remove the walls and suddenly people who can't brake just go flying off the course instead of launching out of the corner in the right direction.  The anti-wall riding penalty in online is stupid. Someone slams into your rear instead of braking and you hit the wall? Five second slowdown penalty. Misjudge your braking zone and slam into the wall, stopping in the process and losing more time than taking it properly would've taken? Five second slowdown penalty. Intentionally go into a corner too fast but pull the handbrake to bounce the rear corner of your car off the wall? No penalty at all. Great system.  Cross Country races are bad. They have been bad since they were introduced in 2. I don't know who thought sweeping right into sweeping left into blind jump was good race design but it isn't. Full throttle for most of the race, and then rewind 15 times because you took the jump at a slightly wrong angle and either didn't land close enough to the checkpoint or you landed in such a way that you will go slamming into a building instead of through the narrow alley the next checkpoint is in. These are bad and they suck, please either stop making them in favor of more proper rally events or at least design them in a way that can be done without rewind.  Half the difficulty options don't even give you more credits anymore. Normal > Sim steering, Manual > M/C, Cosmetic > Full damage, and rewind off don't give more rewards despite taking more skillful play.  I really, really like the horizon series and it's a lot of fun but god does it have flaws some of which are over a decade old. Horizon 5 is still fun and it's absolutely worth the money, but it's not perfect. I really hope 6 brings major improvements to the franchise. Overall 8~9/10

This game has gone through some wild shifts and changes over the years, and it is a battle royale first and foremost above all others, so if that is not your vibe, steer clear.   That said, for a free to play adaptation from a pay to play core, PUBG has thrived since it's initial ups and downs of finding a good foothold in a market that quickly got overtaken by flashier and more cartoony competitors.    This is a great game to just casually knock out a few drops with some friends or goof off in solo que doing self imposed absurd challenges, and the casual mode doubly makes it much less of a chance of just getting completely stomped by people who eat sleep and breath the game while your just trying to play with people of varying skill level and interest in the game.   As it stands now, it is a solid free to play BR option for the people who prefer less cartoony asthetics with more realistic style firearms. It certainly is not a full hardcore vibe on the realistic feel so won't really scratch the itch there, but overall it has a lot going for it in it's specific niche.  The competitive scene is also quite impressive and for such a random variable element of a game that often comes down to luck over skill in terms of equipment strategies, it is still very entertaining to watch in spite of the inherent lack of a certain degree of mechanical balance optimization just due to the nature of the game itself.   There are also very amusing custom lobbies that can be tweaked into all kinds of improvised game modes for very silly group fun if your lucky enough to be part of a community that can muster the numbers to host such a thing!   The journey of improvement and refinement is a constant one that never truly ends however, and these are the things I think could do with some changes to improve the quality of the game and extend it's reach even further:   [b] CASUAL REWORKS [/b]   Change casual ques to 90min instead of 60min and allow groups who are queing together to go off the time remaining of the group member with the most time remaining, even if other group members have 0 time remaining themselves. people meet up and decide to do a little casual play at different points in the day, in different circles, this helps make this process not feel like a time triage excercise similar to scheduling DnD groups   [b] BOT DROP [/b]  Adding a purely co-op comp stomp mode would be very helpful for those of us who enjoy playing casuals but do not want the human competitive element in any way beyond friendly team competition to see who can get the most kills / coolest kills.   Someone like me can go toe to toe easily in the main matches and the "who's a bot and who's not" excitement of casuals is something I can handle easily enough, but for a lot of people I play with who enjoy a purely casual against bots experience that is not high pressure so they can be comfortable and spend time with friends and loved ones without getting upset or too overly stressed, something like this would be much better:   The maps are much smaller environments (they can just be zoomed in sections of already existing maps to start with, but eventually custom designed maps using pre-existing assets would be the best course of action to help with differentation at a glance and variety)   The game mode would be 100 participants, with up to 6 six slots occupied by players in one team replacing a bot spawn from either a pre-que or public lobby (with players still able to launch on less than max numbers)   Everyone parachutes in at the same time in random spots in the sky above the map and have to steer themselves into locations alongside all the bots, and then it's just a free for all as the bots do not have teams, but they always priortize engaging human players over one another (and are generally coded to miss each other as much as possible when fighting one another) they will never kill downed players intentionally, and as the match progresses and the circle tightens, the bots become universally stronger, more well equipped, and deadlier, all while ensuring their top priority is to avoid the closing circle, up to the point of not stopping to engage until they are inside of it at all costs (and also reducing outside of circle damage to the bots so a ton of them don't just die out there like in casuals)   I could elaborate a great deal on more specifics and unique elements of this game mode, but this review only has so much room so if the devs would like to contact me directly, I would happily provide additional expansion and development plans to streamline it's inception!  [b] FAT TRIMMING [/b]    There is soooo much overlapping emergency key jingling from this games years of desperate reinvention and expansion that needs cleaning up. There are so many absurd sub menus and six different currencies doing the same things that could all be solved by one that make the monetized elements far more complex and annoying to engage with.   Making a "give me all my stuff I qualify for" button that just lists a history of where and why a thing was given to the player is so much more effective and gives people a less micro management heavy way of cleanly aquiring things. It should also store and log those qualified rewards until that button IS clicked even if the event or whatever was going on has passed, so that people don't accidentally miss out on things they qualified for simply because of an arbitrary timer.   In addition, make the actual BP shop it's own thing that makes it easier to navigate what is available purely with BP without mixing it with the premium currency shop. You can still put advertisements in the BP shop items directing too premium shop versions, and you can add a premium shop currency buy options for all the BP items too even, but make the designation more clear, and simple to navigate   Again, I have a massive list of UI reconfigurations and changes to offer in great detail, along with many mechanic revisions and refinements, if the developers are interested. I understand the limitations of development especially on a skeleton crewed F2P investment anchor, but I know how to work on nothing budgets with little resources, so happy to offer my expertise if desired!   [b] NO MORE SOLO DANCES [/b]   This one is mildly irksome, but ALL dances of every kind should be group dances. This is a nitpick I will admit it, but it's just unnecissarily exclusionary in a largely team incentivizing game. Add a toggle when activating the dance for it to be solo only if you really want to keep that for more mean spirited players, but don't enforce exclusion.   I could go on an on and on about ideas for new events, tweaks and optimizations, promotional tie ins and baseline improvements but, again, due to limited space here, I'll just end on saying this game is not perfect by far, and it will be infuriating at times both because of the PVP nature of the game, and some of the games baked in elements at it's core, but if you want a slower paced BR That has less frenetic energy than other BR's and Arena Shooters while still being an engaging experience with a bit more of a "real life" influence, this one is the game for you! And it's free, and there are random little events that pop up free game modes to play with so, it's worth keeping installed just to mess around with now and then!

This isn’t just a game. This is an experience.  The atmosphere pulls you in from the very first moments. The world is dark, mythical, beautiful, and at the same time brutally unsettling — the kind that makes you want to keep looking, even when you’re afraid of what’s coming next. Combat is tough, fair, and unforgiving. No mindless button-mashing here. When you win, you know exactly why. When you lose, you do too.  Visually, the game is insane. Every boss feels like a legend, not just another obstacle. The music, animations, and small details all carry weight. And the story? It’s not spoon-fed to you. You have to feel it, piece it together, think about it. That’s what makes it hit harder.  This game isn’t for everyone. It’s demanding, slow where it needs to be, and it doesn’t hold your hand. But if you enjoy a challenge, mythology, and games that take something from you — and then give it back tenfold — this is it.  Highly recommended. Not because it’s “good.” But because it’s different.

I really wish that there was a bit more polish in certain areas and that the first 4/6 chapters were as good as the last 2. I went from not caring about the game at all to actually seeing the strengths of the combat starting at Red Boy/Yaksha, and then thinking that Erlang and the Broken Shell were very well done bosses that showed the best of the game's combat.  Baby Thanos was the hardest boss in the game by far for some reason in chapter 1, due to what you had available to you at the time with limited moves and stats. Yellow Loong also seemed difficult to me at first, but you had way more options to try out and mix things up to win with by that point. Besides those 2 encounters, the difficulty goes way back down and stays consistent.  If the game had better fights like Yaksha, Erlang, and Broken Shell throughout the experience to give more to look forward to, I'd say it'd be ~8.5-9/10. Unfortunately, with how the game is structured and how the majority of the bosses/enemies aren't really a selling point, I have to say the game is overall a 7.5/10. For reference, before the final 2 chapters, my experience was ~6/10 and I didn't understand why people would enjoy it much.  Solid first real game attempt and I thoroughly hope that they learn from it to improve if they make another, especially cause the core game has potential and shows it in brief glimpses at the end.

Some games entertain you. Some impress you. Black Myth: Wukong awakens something ancient in you.  From the first step into its mist-drenched world, this game doesn’t ask for your attention — it commands it. Every stone temple, every whispering forest, every clash of steel feels carved from myth itself. This isn’t just an action RPG. It’s a living legend, retold through sweat, struggle, and triumph.  Combat is pure poetry in motion. Every dodge feels earned, every strike deliberate, every boss a wall you’re meant to break — not with brute force alone, but with patience and respect. When you finally win, it’s not relief you feel. It’s reverence.  The art direction is jaw-dropping. Not flashy for the sake of it, but deeply atmospheric. The world breathes. It watches you. It remembers you. Paired with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack, the game constantly reminds you that you are walking through a story older than time itself.  And Wukong — not just a character, but a force. A symbol of defiance, resilience, and transformation. You don’t merely control him. You become him.  This is a game that trusts the player. It doesn’t hold your hand. It doesn’t rush you. It challenges you — and rewards you with moments that stay with you long after the screen fades to black.  Black Myth: Wukong isn’t trying to be the next big thing. It already is.  If you love myth, mastery, atmosphere, and games that respect your intelligence — this is unmissable.  ! Masterpiece ! ! Myth made playable ! ! A journey worth every struggle !  Recommended without hesitation.

Can be repetitive at times and certain stages are a bit annoying/frustrating (not in a fun way lol) but this game is otherwise amazing. Amazing graphics, super fun bosses, and enough variety with skills/stances/souls to have interesting builds.    I run on a 9600x CPU + Arc B580 GPU + 2x16BG RAM and get around 60-75 FPS usually on very-high/cinematic settings. Ray tracing bumps fps down to 40-60s with some stutter depending on specific settings. Running it might need some trouble shooting for optimization if your not on higher end specs.

I have completed Black Myth: Wukong five times and already unlocked all armor, items, and fully upgraded every ability. However, when I start a new playthrough, the game actually feels harder instead of easier.  Even though my character is at a high level with fully upgraded gear, I die much faster than expected, and enemy damage feels significantly stronger. This feels very frustrating because progression should make the character feel more powerful, not weaker.  After investing many hours into leveling up and collecting everything, I expected a sense of growth and reward. Instead, it feels like the game scales enemies too aggressively, making all upgrades feel meaningless.  I enjoy the world, combat, and overall concept of the game, but this balancing issue seriously affects the replay experience. Please consider adjusting the difficulty scaling so player progression actually matters and feels rewarding.

game_name: Call of Duty®: Black Ops III
review_text: (Single player campaign review) This was the worst Black Ops, let alone Call of Duty game, I have played to this point.  The story of the single player campaign makes no sense, and it is not connected to the first 2 games.  The first 2 missions are used as tutorials and give you a taste of some of the tech abilities you can use within the game.  However, they leave out the names of these abilities.  Plus, they leave out where you can go to equip these abilities in the safehouse.  Example – In the second mission you get to wall run, but if you finish the mission and try to go back and wall run again – you can’t.  I had to look up online to find out where that ability could be equipped in the weapon customizations screen.  Yes, you don’t have to wall run.  You can still cross the area on a platform, but then what is the use of having that ability?  The futuristic setting with the weapons and cybertech available in the game were pretty cool, but that does not make up for how poorly this game was put together.  I’m sure the positive reviews are for the zombies, but I never really cared for those, and multiplayer is just a waste of time these days.  Now I know why Black Ops 4 does not have a single player campaign – no one at Treyarch knows how to write good stories. I would only recommend this game if you like the zombie portion of it.

game_name: Call of Duty®: Black Ops III
review_text: the last worthwhile treyarch zombies experience, albeit one already showing signs of the flaws and user-hostile design decisions that wound up killing call of duty's artistic merit. the campaign is fine, but just fine. there were a couple of quotable moments, but i couldn't tell you what the plot was. realistic difficulty and nightmares mode were fun gimmicks to stretch the replayability of the campaign.  the zombies modding scene is going strong to this day, for what that's worth. common community advice is to always play with third-party security patches, even in singleplayer. i think the game stops awarding you XP if you're using one, but this is okay, because popular patches, or certain workshop mods, implement a better progression system.  the price tag is extortionate. it's been out for 10 years; this game should be open-source, not sold for the same price at which it launched. bundling zombies chronicles with the base game is a good start, but charging collector's edition preorder prices to get all the content in the year of our lord 2026 is sufficient cause to question activision executives' relationship with reality. but of course, you already knew this.  note: my playtime is inaccurate; i have logged hundreds more hours on PS4.
